sections.title: biquad
sections.subtitle: `dsp/biquad.odin` against the RBJ cookbook in C

rows: Butterworth order 8 = 4 sections, section after section (first version)
Butterworth order 8, all sections per sample (what `BiquadCascadeProcess` does now)
stereo, one biquad, both channels in one loop (ns per frame)
state variable filter, low pass, 512 block (ns/sample)

blocks.p: Reading: Odin and gcc generate equally fast loops (the C reference got the same two optimisations). A biquad is a dependency chain from one sample to the next (about 1.8 ns = 6 cycles), so the only ways to go faster are to run independent chains side by side: stereo costs 1.9 ns per frame instead of 3.6 (1.9x), a cascade processed per sample costs 4.1 instead of 7.1 (1.7x). The design is faster in Odin because `core:math` has its own sin / cos / pow while mingw's libm uses the x87 `fsin`.

sections.title: oscillator
sections.subtitle: `dsp/oscillator.odin` against the same algorithms in C

blocks.p: What made the difference (all measured here): (1) a 64 bit fixed point phase wraps by itself, the float `if phase >= 1 { phase -= 1 }` was the whole dependency chain (2.6 -> 1.5 ns for the sine); (2) the block loop works on a local copy of the oscillator, otherwise the compiler stores and reloads the phase around every output store (3x slower); (3) the edge tests are on the integer phase, so the float work and the division only happen in the sample or two around an edge (triangle 2.8 -> 1.1); (4) the sine folds on integers because `floor` is a library call without SSE4.1 (1.5 -> 0.34). Alias suppression (tests with the FFT, Blackman-Harris window, everything not within 8 bins of a harmonic): saw and pulse 15 to 20 dB below the naive shapes at 1 to 9.7 kHz at 48 kHz, triangle 6+ dB.

sections.title: modulation
sections.subtitle: `dsp/envelope.odin`, `dsp/lfo.odin` against the same algorithms in C

rows: ADSR, linear segments, gate toggling so all stages run
LFO triangle (the Odin one also has the phase offset and unipolar switch)

blocks.p: The block procs run on a local copy of the state and the LFO block has the shape as a compile time constant, as in the oscillator.

sections.title: resample
sections.subtitle: `dsp/resample.odin` against the WDL resampler of REAPER, sinc mode, float samples, g++ -O2

columns.name: case
columns.unit: ns per output sample, blocks of 512 input samples

blocks.p: Not equal designs: when the rate goes down the Odin kernel is stretched by the ratio (so 96 -> 44.1 reads 2.2 times more taps, which is what keeps its stopband the same at every ratio: measured -88 / -127 / -121 dB for a tone above the new Nyquist, LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH), WDL always reads its fixed number of taps. For up conversion and equal rates both read the same number of taps and the Odin one is 20 to 45% slower. First version 2x slower still (74 ns for HIGH): the fixed point table position (an integer add per tap instead of a float multiply, convert and abs), the (value, difference) pair table (one load) and four independent sums (one float add chain costs the latency of an add per tap) gave the 2x. What is left is the gather of the table (no SIMD gather on the SSE2 baseline); a polyphase bank per ratio with contiguous coefficients would vectorize, at the cost of rebuilding it when the ratio changes (not worth it at 40 ns per output sample: a 48 kHz mono stream costs 0.2% of a core).

sections.title: fft
sections.subtitle: `dsp/fft.odin` against KissFFT, pffft, WDL and FFTW

blocks.p: The vector stages (`core:simd`, 4 floats = two complex values per vector, twiddles from a pair table, one shuffle per butterfly pair, unaligned loads) are 20 to 25% faster; 1024 points is about 27 GFlops by the 5 N log2 N convention. What is left is memory traffic (one pass per radix-2 stage: a radix-4 stage would halve it) and the bit reversal.

Against the C libraries (`odin run tools/bench -- fft`, gcc -O2; FFTW 3.3.10 built as a static float library with SSE2/AVX/AVX2 codelets and `FFTW_MEASURE` plans, out of place; pffft SSE, KissFFT, the WDL FFT; Odin = AVX2 level, ns per transform; ratio = Odin / C, below 1 = Odin faster):

Honest reading: ahead of KissFFT and WDL, but 1.4 to 1.8x behind pffft (complex) and 3x (real), and 3.4 to 4.7x behind FFTW, which is the reference for "as fast as it gets". Why: the transform here is radix-2 with a scalar bit reversal and scalar first stages (every stage is a pass over memory), pffft and FFTW use radix-4 / split-radix style passes on data in a split layout (all real parts, all imaginary parts) so that every vector lane does useful work and the shuffles disappear, and the real transform's pass over the bins is scalar here.

sections.title: dynamics
sections.subtitle: `dsp/dynamics.odin` against the same algorithms in C

blocks.p: The C compressor calls libm `log10f` / `powf` per sample (the mingw ones: 50 to 150 ns, it varied between builds of the same code); the Odin one uses `FastLog2` / `FastExp2` (a polynomial of the mantissa and the exponent bits: 1.5e-5 dB and 1e-7 relative error, tested), 31 ns before that change with `core:math`. The limiter: rings addressed with masks instead of `%` (4.1 -> 4.1 against C's 3.9 -> 2.1 once C got the same change), the per sample scalars in a local copy for the block (the arrays share the struct with the output as far as the compiler knows, 5.7 -> 2.5 together with the masks).

sections.title: sampler
sections.subtitle: `dsp/sampler.odin` against the same voice in C

columns.name: case
columns.unit: ns per output sample, stereo sample into a stereo output, cubic

blocks.p: `math.floor` is a library call on the default x86-64 target (no SSE4.1), which cost the pitch 1.0 case 25%: the positions are never negative, so the voice truncates instead. `dsp/wav.odin` (header parsing and decoding of 8 / 16 / 24 / 32 bit PCM and 32 / 64 bit float, extensible headers, truncated files) has tests but no benchmark: decoding is a loop over memory.

The state variable filter's block loop advances its two states as a 2x2 matrix times the states plus the input (the same arithmetic with the intermediate values substituted): the chain from one sample to the next is one multiply and two adds, 3.1 -> 2.1 ns per sample (it was 1.3 times slower than C before). The crossover keeps its four sections in scalars of the loop (two independent chains): 4.5 -> 2.1 ns. (The same trick on the biquad does not help: its chain is already one multiply and one subtract.)

sections.title: meter
sections.subtitle: `dsp/meter.odin` against the same algorithms in C

rows: true peak, 4x oversampled, 24 taps per phase (ns/sample)

blocks.p: The loudness meter is 1.5 times slower than C and stays so: its cost is two biquads in series per channel (one chain of two latencies per channel), the C reference interleaves the two channels in one loop and the pair loop of the Odin version did not change that (4.4 -> 3.9 -> 4.1 ns per frame over three versions). At 4 ns per frame it is 0.2% of a core per stereo stream at 48 kHz; not worth more. The true peak uses a doubled history (a sample is stored twice so the 24 sample window is contiguous), vectorized by the compiler.

sections.title: convolution
sections.subtitle: `dsp/convolution.odin`: partitioned FFT convolution, against direct convolution in C

blocks.p: Not the same algorithm: the table shows where they cross (a direct convolution costs 0.33 ns per tap and sample here, the partitioned one is almost independent of the length: 35 ns per sample for a one second impulse response with 1024 sample partitions, at a latency of 1024 samples; B = 256 has a quarter of the latency and three times the cost at one second). Exactness: against the definition in f64 to 2e-6 sqrt(length) for lengths 1 to 24000 (float transforms), and the output is the same whatever block sizes it is fed.

sections.title: oversample
sections.subtitle: `dsp/oversample.odin`, 47 tap half band filters, against the same algorithm in C

columns.name: case
columns.unit: ns per original sample, up and down

blocks.p: The history is stored twice (at `position` and `position + length`) so the filter window is contiguous without a modulo or a shift: 14.4 -> 11.1 ns. The C reference shifts its history with memmove (the simplest correct version). Measured aliasing of a hard clipper on a 3 kHz tone: 4x oversampling takes more than 20 dB out of it (test); the pair delays 23 / 34.5 / 40.25 samples for 2x / 4x / 8x (`OversamplerLatency`).

sections.title: simd
sections.subtitle: `dsp/cpu.odin`: the kernel sets of this machine against each other, `odin run tools/bench -- --no-c simd`

blocks.p: The baseline is what the compiler targets (SSE2, 4 floats); AVX2 + FMA is chosen at run time when CPUID and XGETBV say the CPU and the operating system have it (`plan.level`).
The bit reversal, the first radix 4 stage and the real transform's pass over the bins are still scalar, which is why the FFT gains less than the 2x of the vector width.

sections.title: Tried and dropped: AVX2 gather resampler
sections.subtitle: benchmark/simd, 2026-11-16

blocks.p: A 8-tap gather kernel (vgatherdps twice per 8 taps, FMA) for the resampler tap sum was 15 to 20% slower than the scalar four-sum loop at every quality and ratio (MEDIUM 0.9187: 27.8 -> 32.8 ns per input sample), so it was removed. A polyphase bank (contiguous dot products) only works for a fixed integer step, i.e. upsampling by a rational ratio.

sections.title: fft, second round
sections.subtitle: Stockham radix 4 on split data, `dsp/fft_planar_amd64.odin`; out of place `FftForwardTo` / real transforms read and write the caller arrays directly

blocks.p: The gap to FFTW went from 3.4 - 4.7x to 1.3 - 1.8x. What changed: no bit reversal (the Stockham passes put the outputs in order), split layout (a vector is eight complex values, a complex multiply has no shuffle), radix 4 passes (half the memory traffic), twiddles broadcast per butterfly group, the real transforms working directly on the caller arrays. FFTW still wins by its hand scheduled codelets that keep a whole 16 - 64 point sub transform in registers (fewer passes over memory, no first pass transposition) and by planning (it measures several algorithms on this machine).

LLVM tunes for a generic x86-64 CPU and emits every unaligned 256 bit load / store as two 128 bit halves (vmovups xmm + vinsertf128). `@(enable_target_feature="...,-slow-unaligned-mem-32")` on the AVX2 kernels removes it.

blocks.p: Bounds checks (`#no_bounds_check` on the kernels, lengths are validated once) and the unaligned split were the two causes of 2 - 4x slower first numbers.

sections.subtitle: `dsp/vmath.odin` against the C library functions, mingw msvcrt expf / logf / tanhf / sinf / cosf, 2048 samples; the Odin numbers include the loop that prepares the input

blocks.p: Accuracy against f64: exp 3e-7 relative, log 3e-7 + 1.5e-7 |ln x|, tanh 3e-7, sin / cos 3e-7 for |x| < 100 and 1e-5 up to 8000; the 4 and 8 lane versions are bit identical (tested).

sections.title: fft of any length
sections.subtitle: `dsp/fft_any.odin` against FFTW 3.3.10, ns per complex transform

blocks.p: The mixed radix butterflies are scalar (radix 2, 4, 3, 5 written out, other primes generic); the cost model picks Bluestein on the AVX2 power of two FFT when it is cheaper. A planar AVX2 mixed radix kernel like the power of two one is the way to close the gap.

sections.title: fft of any length, second round: AVX2 mixed radix kernel
sections.subtitle: `dsp/fft_mixed_amd64.odin`, lengths 2^a 3^b 5^c

sections.title: fft of any length, third round: radix 7 and 128 bit passes
sections.subtitle: `dsp/fft_mixed_amd64.odin`, lengths 2^a 3^b 5^c 7^d

blocks.p: Sizes with a single factor 2 or 4 (1764 = 4 9 49, 44100) had every odd pass at a stride of 4, 12, 36, ... that is not a multiple of 8, so they ran as scalar code. A 4 lane pass (`pass_narrow`, twiddles broadcast, the butterflies generic over the vector type) takes them, and a radix 7 butterfly (3 sums, 3 differences, 3 + 3 fused multiply-add chains) completes the 7 smooth sizes. ns per complex forward transform, Odin `-o:speed` against FFTW:
Still behind: sizes with factors of 11 or more (Bluestein), and sizes with no factor 2 (the first pass is at stride 1 and scalar).

sections.title: fft of any length, fourth round: radix 11 and 13, the flat pass
sections.subtitle: `dsp/fft_mixed_amd64.odin`, lengths 2^a 3^b 5^c 7^d 11^e 13^f

blocks.p: A generic odd radix butterfly (sums and differences of the pairs x_k, x_(R-k), R / 2 table entries of cos and sin) serves 11 and 13. Passes now run by kind: 8 lane (stride a multiple of 8), 4 lane (a multiple of 4), and the **flat pass** for everything else (odd strides, stride 2, the first pass of lengths with no factor 4): the elements of a pass are the flat indices at = s p + q, the inputs of one butterfly are at + k n / R, so eight consecutive indices are plain vector loads whatever the stride; the twiddles are one table entry per flat index and only the stores scatter, through a small buffer. ns per complex forward transform, `-o:speed`, against FFTW (same machine, same run):
Still slow: lengths with a prime factor of 17 or more (scalar mixed radix or Bluestein, which is ahead of FFTW for primes themselves).

sections.title: fft, the benchFFTS matrix and FFTS
sections.subtitle: 2026-11-17, `odin run tools/bench -- fft`, AVX2 level, gcc -O2, ns per transform, ratio = Odin / C, below 1 = Odin faster

blocks.p: Added after the benchFFTS reference (the bench program of FFTS: forward and backward, complex and real, 2 to 262144): FFTS (linkotec fork, static, SSE + run time generated code) as a fifth library; the cases `complexb` (backward), `complexip` (in place forward, the copy of the input is in the time for the libraries that need it), `realb` (c2r; FFTW and Odin copy the destroyed spectrum back every run), complex sizes 2 to 2^20 (every power of two) and real sizes 4 to 2^18. Libraries that do not support a size are skipped (pffft complex < 16, real < 32; WDL < 16 / 32).

Honest reading: the pffft ratio is below 1 everywhere it runs (complex 0.3 to 0.85, real 0.5 to 0.7 above 64 points). Against FFTS and FFTW from 256 points up Odin is faster or equal except the backward complex transform against FFTW at 256 to 4096 (1.1 to 1.2; forward is 0.94 to 1.04 there). What the matrix revealed: below 64 points (2 to 32 for complex, 4 to 32 for real) both FFTS and FFTW win, by 2 to 4x at the smallest sizes (FFTS 16: 5.8 ns, ours 12.1), because their unrolled codelets have no plan loop; the small real transforms (16: 4x FFTS) and the backward real transform (64: 1.9x FFTS) are the weakest rows. The earlier tables had no size below 64. Next step: unrolled codelets for 2 to 32 (complex) and 4 to 32 (real), then a look at the backward pass at 256 to 4096.

Straight line scalar transforms for complex 2, 4, 8 and real 4, 8, 16 (forward and backward), ns per transform before -> after (FFTS in brackets): complex 2: 3.2 -> 2.2 (2.0); 4: 8.3 -> 3.0 (1.8); 8: 7.8 -> 3.6 (2.6); real 4: 12.6 -> 4.0 (8.3); 8: 18.7 -> 5.1 (9.1); 16: 28.7 -> 10.8 (7.3); real backward 4: 10.5 -> 4.5 (2.6); 8: 16.4 -> 5.9 (4.0); 16: 24.2 -> 12.3 (6.1). A scalar 16 point complex transform (18.8 ns) was slower than the SIMD path (12.1 ns): not used. Still behind FFTS: complex 16 (13.6 against 5.8) and 32 (19.4 against 13.8), real 32 (45.8 against 12.8): they need SIMD codelets. Real 32 added to the codelets (the half size 16 network is scalar, the pass over the bins is straight line): 45.8 -> 26.5 ns forward, 40.9 -> 26.2 backward (FFTS 12.8 / 12.5). Complex 16 and 32 stay on the SIMD kernels.

`complexb` first copied the input and ran the in place `FftInverse`, while the forward case used the out of place `FftForwardTo` (and FFTW both out of place): the 1.1 - 1.5x "backward gap" was that copy. `FftInverseTo` (out of place, the planar kernel reads and writes the caller's arrays) is now the backward case; backward = forward within 2 % at every size. Against FFTW (out of place, AVX2 codelets, ratio Odin / FFTW, two runs of the whole matrix, timer noise 10 - 15 %): 64: 1.23 - 1.28, 128: 1.14, 256: 1.05 - 1.07 (88 against 80 ns in the quiet runs), 512: 1.11, 1024: 0.92 - 0.97, 2048: 1.07, 4096: 1.04 - 1.07, 8192 and up: 0.76 - 0.89. The AVX-512 level (this machine, FFTW has no AVX-512 codelets) is 1.2 to 1.5x faster than the AVX2 kernels here (`FFT_LEVEL=avx2` in the benchmark: 256: 107 against 88, 1024: 490 against 320, 4096: 2700 against 1870). What is left is 64 and 256 points (10 - 25 % behind FFTW): register resident AVX-512 kernels would close it.

At 64 points the transposing store of the first radix 4 pass writes exactly the four 16 value runs the second pass loads, and the second pass' stores are the third pass' loads, so the three passes run on eight register pairs with no store to load round trip: complex 64 forward 29.0 -> 15.0 ns, backward 29 -> 15.0, in place (with the input copy) 37.7 -> 25 (FFTW 23 out of place, FFTS 28, pffft 50). 128 and 256 points do not line up this way (the second pass reads from streams n / 4 apart, which different iterations of the first pass wrote).

Complex 16 is two vector registers (real parts, imaginary parts): a radix 4 over the 128 bit chunks, the twiddles, a radix 4 over the lanes (both as shuffles plus a combination with constants per chunk / lane), one shuffle to natural order. Complex 32 = a radix 2 step and two of those; real 32 and 64 run the pass over the bins in the same registers (the partner bin is a lane reversal). ns per transform before -> after (FFTS in brackets): complex 16: 13.6 -> 5.5 (5.8), 32: 19.4 -> 11.8 (13.8), backward the same; real 32: 26.5 -> 8.7 (12.8), real 64: 38 -> 17 (about 27). The backward real cases of the benchmark copy the spectrum before every run and pay a store forwarding penalty for it (realb 32: 22.6 with the copy, 7.7 without; 64: 29.4 against 14.5); the kernels do not destroy their input.

The 64 point transform (three radix 4 passes in registers) is a function of eight split vectors (`fft64_core`); two of them and a radix 2 step make 128 points (`fft_avx512_128`), two 128 point ones make 256 (`fft_avx512_256`, 32 vectors live, some spill), and the pass over the bins of the real transforms (`real_post` / `real_pre`, bin k pairs with N / 2 - k, a lane reversal across the blocks of sixteen) runs on the same registers for real 64, 128 and 256. ns per transform before -> after (FFTW out of place AVX2, FFTS): complex 128: 42 -> 28.2 (FFTW 40, FFTS 29); complex 256: 90 -> 77.4 (FFTW 80, FFTS 98); real 128: 37.6 -> 21; real 256: 74 -> 44; backward the same as forward for the complex sizes (the real backward rows of the benchmark include the spectrum copy: 128: 32, 256: 50).

The "padded convolution Rader" idea for primes whose p - 1 has a large factor comes to the same convolution as Bluestein (2 p - 3 against 2 p - 1 points), so the gain is in the size of that convolution: Bluestein used a power of two (4099: 8197 -> 16384, twice the work) and now takes the cheapest size the mixed SIMD kernel runs between 2 n - 1 and the next power of two (4099: 8960 = 2^8 5 7, 0.55 ns per point), plus SIMD chirp multiplications (and the 1 / m scale folded into the output chirp). ns, before -> after (FFTW): 4099: 43591 -> 19124 (17949); 74: 583 -> 262 (536); 222: 1269 -> 769 (1560); 323: 2297 -> 1490 (2579); 646: 4884 -> 2818 (5266); 1517: 10464 -> 5634 (21291). The measured speed of the mixed kernel by size is in the comment of `bluestein_length` (8192: 0.53 ns per point, 8400: 0.63, 8232 = 2^3 3 7^3: 0.75).

The AVX-512 kernel's pass list (radix 4, 4, then radix 8, `fft_planar512_init`) run with 8 lane vectors (`butterfly8`, `pass_wide_radix8`: 16 inputs, 16 outputs and the twiddles against 16 vector registers, so the butterfly spills): complex, AVX2 level, ns before -> after: 64: 33 -> 34, 128: 59 -> 66, 256: 109 -> 123, 512: 237 -> 252, 1024: 484 -> 529, 2048: 1197 -> 1309, 4096: 2739 -> 2804, 8192: 6456 -> 6547: 5 to 13 % slower, the saved trip through memory costs less than the spills. The AVX2 level stays 1.2 to 1.6x behind FFTW at 32 .. 8192 points (FFTW 64: 21, 1024: 399, 4096: 1831; ours 33, 484, 2739); it is the kernel with the most room on machines without AVX-512.

Rebuilt `benchmark/fft` with FFTW 3.3.11 (3.3.10 before; its build needs -mavx2 -mfma for the new avx2-128 codelets) and `ENABLE_AVX512=ON`: complex out of place, ns: 64: 20.2, 256: 72.5, 1024: 324, 4096: 1739, 16384: 12.2 us, 65536: 74.4 us (3.3.10 without AVX-512: 21.4, 78, 351, 1821, 12.7, 78). Ours at the AVX-512 level: 14.8, 70, 320, 1866, 9.5, 52: ahead at 64, 16384, 65536, level at 256 and 1024, 7 % behind at 4096. IPP and KFR remain the references that matter (see the roadmap).

Skipping one pass at a time (garbage output, timing only), complex 1024: all passes 321 ns, without pass 0 (stride 1, deinterleave, transposing store) 219, without pass 1 (stride 4) 232: the two small stride passes are 60 % of the time (4096: 1894 total, 1439 / 1437 without them: 48 %); the two radix 8 passes are the rest. A four step matrix kernel with 512 bit vectors (16 x 64: radix 16 across rows, twiddles, one 8 x 8 complex transposition, radix 64 across vectors as 8 x 8) takes 355 - 364 ns (321 for the planar one); AVX2 16 x 64 at 1024 takes 631 - 830 against 475 (the first and the last radix 64 are the cost). Not kept. What is still open for 1024 .. 4096 is to remove the stride 1 and 4 passes' two transposing stores in another way (a radix 16 first pass with one transposition; sizes above L1 with a blocked plan).
